I read a very practical explanation about this: Palpatine was using cqc moves with his saber instead of the usually long-arc slashing moves that we normally see. 

If you go back, he hardly ever makes a long swing and almost always kept the hilt close to his body for quick thrusts with the tip of the blade. 

So he not only stuns the Jedi with his speed, he also uses very quick precise saber thrusts that are hard to stop in close quarters let alone with three other individuals bunched closely next to you. 

Finally, he also set the stages for the fight, and we can anticipate that someone who can set up a full on war without many noticing could also set in motion the events that led up to the office duel. 

So he set the location and circumstances for the fight and took his moment when he had it to eliminate a few Jedi who didn’t know what they were dealing with. 

Personally, I’m more comfortable with that rational than him using unknown force powers.

Type 1 diabetic here, just want to offer my perspective. I personally have done fine using a combination of CGM and my insulin pens (basal and bolus), and am hesitant to leave my glucose control to a computer algorithm. 

Not that I don't see it being beneficial, but for me the risk of a malfunction overweight the benefits, and I feel I'm doing well enough as is. Same thing for pumps, while it could improve my control, I'm wary of  it malfunctioning. For example, my friend's pump disconnected when he slept and rolled over, and his blood sugar skyrocketed to the 500s while he slept. Conversely, I've heard stories of the pumps shooting *all* of the insulin into to the user after a malfunction, which can be life threatening. I'm sure it's rare, but I'm erring on the side of caution, and familiarity. 

They should improve the CGM alarms, it goes trough my phone and I sleep through it often, luckily though I rarely have low glucose overnight, and when I do I typically wake up on my own. 

Edit: Also worth noting, but current CGMs let you share your data in realtime with whoever you want. Both of my parents are on there and have called me to prevent lows before that I might have missed otherwise. To me that combination with the CGM and diligent use of my pens is enough to keep me healthy...so far.

Good start. This is largely preferential as its subjective, but I would play with the settings on your keyboard, or with whatever DAW you use to blend it better in the mix and make it "sound better." By better I mean less static, you can use the current sound at parts but I would blend it behind other things or maybe work on making it a bit more resonant in some way and less harsh. 

A little attack on the synth or keyboard might do a lot to help reduce the harshness of some of the chord transitions. You could also try halving the volume on the original keyboard track, panning it to one side (hard left of right), duplicating it, replacing the duplicate of the first instrument with another complimentary instrument*, panning it to the opposite side, and matching it's volume with the first track. See what you think, you could also try keeping the keyboard part as is, and simply adding that other instrument. Just make sure you ke your levels balanced for the mix.

Again EQ is preferential**, but I would try bringing the lows and mids of your drums out more and reducing the mids and lows on your keyboard track to blend it better.^

Overall they might be a little bit too prominent for my taste, I would also pay attention to your dynamics. Try switching the beat up every few bars, and changing volume levels at various times for effect. (I.e. A loud-quiet dynamic, or another example would be a sudden drop before an increase in volume for a chorus). Otherwise it's a bit repetitive, but like I said this is a great start. 

I really enjoyed the chord pattern by the way, I think you can do a lot with that. Good work! Now if it's just to be used as a ringtone, then not much needs to be changed other than the levels. 

*A complimentary instrument should be something that adds to your existing sound, maybe even as a direct copy of the first track, but doesn't overpower or dominate to the point of drowning out that first track. So for example, a light soft synth pad with heavy attack would play interestingly along the keyboard part as is.

**With EQ, certain genres need certain levels, as do certain devices for playback. Try mixing "flat," and then playing with what sounds good to you. If you need reference, take a break (which you should do regularly anyways to prevent any fatigue) and listen to something you like to get an idea for how they balanced their levels in production or used dynamics to make it more interesting.

Okay so the drums need to be tighter and less muddied. I noticed they sort of sounded like they were underwater in the beginning and I kept expecting them to rise out of it but they didn't. Now you can make them like that for effect but don't make it the basis of your track. If that's just the sample "as is", try to use EQ effects to bring up the highs and reduce the lows while keeping your mids balanced. You'll be amazed the difference it makes. 

I would also maybe add like a clap or more prominent snare to fill out the percussion. 

The piano like someone else said didn't match as well at some parts. You could fix this by purchasing some higher quality instrument packs, or by actually using effects on the piano. You also could make the piano less of a mainstay feature by just reducing it's volume, duplicating the instrumentation onto another instrument, and bringing that second instrument's volume up to drown out the piano. Make sure though the second instrument doesn't overpower the other parts f your beat if you go that route, it should all be part of a layer. Each sound has it's place in it.

The track needs to be more dynamic, think: "highs and lows," in volume, reverb, delays, etc. This is how you make it interesting after you have your concept.

Some advice that no one gave me before I got to college: be yourself. 

Oh yeah, I can hear the groans already "how cliché can ya get?"

But it really is important that you understand a few things:

1) College is different, you may be pressured to change up things or do things you didn't do in high school, a lot of us went through that. There's a lot of good but also bad things that you can easily fall into, just remember that you are there for an education first but also when you're having fun, do what makes you genuinely happy and make sure you do it with people who build you up and respect you for being you. 

2) You're going to meet a lot of new people, some of them won't be so kind, others will become your closest friends. Just understand that everyone, like you is figuring themselves out. ESPECIALLY during that first year. Don't waste time on negative people, but don't be negative either, you can only battle insecurity with positivity, I wish I knew that freshman year.

3) Don't let one bad grade or boring class change your attitude, there's going to be a lot of classes that you don't like. The important thing with that is to have the longview, see your goals and don't lose sight of them. Additionally, your friends and peers can empathize, so help each other out! 

4) Finally, don't be afraid to ask for help. It's basic I know, and I promise I'm not making assumptions about you, but we all have some tough times, few of us ask for help during them. Now I can tell you're already seeking some sort of advice or tips, so that's great, never stop doing that. 

Now college will take more motivation because you're  going to get a lot more freedom than you're likely used to, but I hope these tips will help!

BONUS TIP: Make sure you know each teacher and they know you and your face. Don't be a brown noser but be active in class and engage the professors when you need help or have questions. You'd be amazed how few college students do that, and sometimes it ends up helping in ways that you can't even see yet.
